apush-mcq-0139.reason: Image shows sick people covered in spots lying helpless on mats, whole households struck at once. A (deliberate weapon) is not shown; C (from Africa) contradicts the standard account; D (immunity) contradicts the image.

apush-mcq-0140.reason: No immunity after thousands of years apart is why disease outranked weapons. A is wrong (guns mattered but were not decisive alone); B is wrong (Native peoples fought hard); C is wrong (smallpox hit during the 1520 siege).

apush-mcq-0141.reason: Smallpox killed defenders including the emperor Cuitlahuac and left the city too weak to hold out.

apush-mcq-0142.reason: Passage says the crown spent silver on armies and interest while prices rose at home.

apush-mcq-0143.reason: Passage says prices rose across Europe as more silver money circulated.

apush-mcq-0144.reason: Passage's conclusion: wealth arrived and left again; prosperity depends on use, not the amount.

apush-mcq-0145.reason: Protestant rivals translated and printed it to use against Catholic Spain.

apush-mcq-0146.reason: Las Casas's vivid account, the printing press, and rivals eager to discredit Spain together made the Legend.

apush-mcq-0147.reason: Passage says the English presented their own colonies as godly and humane.

apush-mcq-0148.reason: Wealth (Asian trade, gold, silver) is the most significant cause; D is only one part of the economic motive.

apush-mcq-0149.reason: Passage says the old land routes grew costlier and less certain after 1453.

apush-mcq-0150.reason: Portugal already had an African sea route to Asia; Spain had none, which is why Spain backed Columbus's westward gamble.

apush-saq-0031.a: Prices rose across Europe as silver money circulated, and the Spanish crown grew poorer rather than richer despite the silver inflows.
apush-saq-0031.b: The silver was spent on armies, ships, and interest on heavy borrowing, and taxes rose more than fivefold to pay for wars; it was not invested in farms or workshops, so it left Spain again.
apush-saq-0031.c: Prices rose across Europe as the supply of silver money grew (inflation beyond Spain).

apush-saq-0032.a: Columbus saw the Taino as harmless, unarmed people who did not know weapons and would make fine servants, easily subjugated.
apush-saq-0032.b: It shows Spanish aims were conquest and control: to subjugate Native peoples and make them do whatever the Spanish wanted, i.e., exploit their labor.
apush-saq-0032.c: The entry is Columbus's own account, written to justify his voyage to the crown, so it is one-sided and self-serving; it also survives only as copied by Las Casas, and it gives no Taino perspective.

apush-saq-0033.a: Hispaniola's Native population fell from over 1,000,000 in 1492 to about 500 in the 1540s; across the Americas populations fell an estimated 50 to 90 percent between 1500 and 1650.
apush-saq-0033.b: Old World diseases such as smallpox, to which Native peoples had no immunity (the table itself does not name a cause, so this draws on outside knowledge; warfare and forced labor also contributed).
apush-saq-0033.c: The collapse of the Native labor force pushed Spain to bring in enslaved Africans and to intensify coerced labor systems (also outside the stimulus).

leq_outline.thesis: Disease was the most significant cause of Spanish success in conquering the Americas, to a large extent: it devastated Native populations and crippled resistance. But it was not sufficient alone; steel, horses, and Native allies were necessary partners, so disease was greatest but not sole.
leq_outline.context: Spanish conquest of Mexico and Peru; the Columbian Exchange; Native societies before contact, separated from Old World germs for thousands of years.
evidence: Smallpox in Tenochtitlan in 1520 killed the emperor Cuitlahuac and weakened the defense during the siege.
Native populations fell 50 to 90 percent between 1500 and 1650.
Native peoples had no immunity after thousands of years apart.
leq_outline.complexity: Disease worked with steel, horses, and Native allies rather than acting alone; it was the greatest single cause but not the only one.
